title: Ammar ibn Yasir
hook: son of Sumayyah and Yasir, forced under torture to speak against his faith, and told by the Prophet ﷺ that his heart was what mattered (16:106)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Dharr, plain words and a long walk alone. Your line was walked alone. What true thing did you say, plainly and kindly? Day eight hundred twenty-six.

Medina, the early days. The believers are building their mosque with their own hands, carrying mud bricks from where they're made to where the walls are going up. One brick each, trip after trip. One man is carrying two at a time. He's covered in dust. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops, and with his own hand brushes the dust from the man's head. His name is Ammar. And before, back in Mecca, this same man broke. Today: Ammar ibn Yasir, and the heart that held.
screen: `BUILDING THE MOSQUE BY HAND.` → `ONE MAN CARRIES TWO BRICKS.` → `THE PROPHET BRUSHES OFF THE DUST.`

segments.voice: We met his family on an earlier day: his mother Sumayyah and his father Yasir, tortured in Mecca for their faith. Ammar was tortured too, and pushed until he said what his captors demanded, words against the Prophet. A report in al-Hakim says he came to the Prophet weeping, and was asked one question: how do you find your heart? At peace with faith, he said. And he was told: if they come back to it, say it again. Commentators connect this with a verse in Surah an-Nahl. In Pickthall's translation, it excuses the one who disbelieves under force: "save him who is forced thereto and whose heart is still content with the Faith." Both are there: the words forced out of him, and the mercy. Now look at what came after. The scene with the bricks is in Sahih al-Bukhari: everyone carried one, and Ammar carried two, and the Prophet brushed the dust from him. The man who broke under torture did not spend his life as a broken man. He carried double. Another report in Bukhari has the companion Abu al-Darda describing Ammar as the one whom God protected from Satan on the tongue of His Prophet. Protected. That's how the people around him remembered him: not by his worst moment, but by what was said over him afterward. Ammar's story doesn't pretend the moment didn't happen. The words were said; the verse speaks to them. What it refuses is to let that moment define the whole man. The heart held. The rest of him got up, and carried bricks.
screen: `FORCED TO SAY THE WORDS.` · `HOW DO YOU FIND YOUR HEART?` · `TWO BRICKS AT A TIME.` · `PROTECTED, ON THE TONGUE OF HIS PROPHET.` · then, large: `THE HEART HELD.`

segments.voice: This week went from Hasan and Husayn and the people of the house to Bilal, Salman, Abu Dharr and Ammar. Now the practice: forgive yourself one moment of weakness. Sit, and breathe. Let one moment come back, a time you gave in, said the wrong thing, didn't hold. Don't argue with it. Then ask the question he was asked: how do you find your heart? What did you really want, underneath? Let that answer be true too. If you pray, you can ask God's forgiveness and mercy. If not, just set the moment down beside you, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Ammar, forced under torture to speak against his faith, told his heart was what mattered, and remembered carrying double the bricks for the mosque. Today's word.
Your line: the heart held. Today, after one moment you're not proud of, skip the replay; ask what your heart wanted, and carry on with the next good thing. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Muslim jurists cite Ammar's story and Qur'an 16:106 for the ruling that someone forced under threat to speak against their faith, while the heart stays with it, is not held guilty, and Muslims remember Ammar with honor among the early believers.

original.note: Arabic: Ammar, son of Yasir; his mother was Sumayyah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a companion who once denied his faith.
what it means: a man forced to speak under torture whose heart held, and who went on to carry double at the building of the mosque.
what a scholar hears: the weeping report is in al-Hakim, commentators tie it to 16:106, and Bukhari keeps both the bricks and Abu al-Darda's words about him.
